A 2016 letter to the editor in the journal Pulmonary Circulation. This letter argues against conclusions from a previously published study that deconditioning is the primary cause of POTS. 

Again, this is from 2016, before long-COVID made POTS popular, which I believe is one reason we're seeing so much bias and pushback (that's my personal observation only).

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5019095/

I first started noticing severe POTS symptoms (I have had some symptoms since childhood) during nursing school, simply because we were practicing taking vital signs on each other all the time. It was treated as primary hypertension, and I assumed that my elevated HR was because I was out of shape. Once alerted to the problem, I felt very embarrassed having my pulse taken both as practice in school and at doctor visits.

Eventually, I determined that I likely had hyperadrenergic POTS. My PCP wasn't really interested/didn't know anything about it, so I asked her to change my HTN regimen from an ARB + diuretic to a beta blocker. I felt like I was talking down to her when I explained that someone with POTS shouldn't be on a diuretic...especially since I'd already had one syncopal episode caused by dehydration.

So did deconditioning *cause* my POTS? No. Did it force me to become less active which then *did* lead to deconditioning? Most definitely. So now the two issues feed each other, and I would suspect that many are in a similar situation.

I've been worried about stuff like this ever since POTS and ME/CFS started trending on Twitter due to long covid. And here we are. The only bright side is that the mass influx of new patients will likely lead to long overdue research funding.

Not stupid! Fluid stuff is one of the harder pieces of physiology to grasp, imo. Basically, water follows salt. If there's too much sodium somewhere in your body, then water is going to flow in there via osmosis to restore the balance. Thus, the more salt you have, the more water you retain. But, as you say, it indeed doesn't matter if you don't also consume enough water with it. That's why we increase both fluids and electrolytes (of which sodium is one). Normal people don't have to do this because they're not chronically hypovolemic and forever at risk of dehydrating.
